items.statement:
Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link with chosen disjoint smooth normal tubes, and let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth embedded spanning surfaces with boundary $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily. Supply radial collar coordinates in the tubes in which each surface collar is given by a smooth ray direction depending on the boundary parameter. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and orient each torus of $\partial\nu L$ as the boundary of the oriented solid tube, so its outward normal points into $X$. Orient the two surface boundary curves on those tori compatibly with $L$.

Let $\alpha$ be a smoothly and properly embedded arc of transverse intersection of $F_0\cap X$ and $F_1\cap X$, transverse to $\partial X$, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially through the supplied collars to the corresponding points of $L$, obtaining a smooth embedded arc $A$. Assume a neighborhood of this extended arc contains no other intersection components. Write $i_0,i_1\in\{1,-1\}$ for the ordered local intersection signs of the two boundary curves at its endpoints, measured on $\partial\nu L$.

The union $F_0\cup F_1$ has a closed intrinsic neighborhood $K$ of $A$ modeled by four pages with common arc, glued at each end by one of the matchings $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$, with pages zero and two on $F_0$ and pages one and three on $F_1$. The two end matchings differ if and only if $i_0=i_1$. Consequently collapsing $A$ in this neighborhood gives a closed topological disk exactly when $i_0+i_1=2$ or $-2$. When $i_0+i_1=0$ it gives two disks joined at their interior centers. For the standard cases the ambient arc-collapse map can be chosen supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $A$, and its image of $K$ is an embedded topological disk. Local flatness of that disk is not asserted here.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Take four rectangles $P_j=[0,1]_t\times[0,1]_r$, $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Identify their edges $r=0$ pointwise in the $t$ coordinate to a common arc $A$. At each end $t=e$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, also identify the radial edges pointwise in $r$ by a matching $\mu_e$, where each $\mu_e$ is one of $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$. Let $K$ be this finite quotient complex, and let $C$ be the image of the four outer edges $r=1$.

If the two end matchings differ, then $K/A$ is a closed topological disk whose boundary is exactly the image of $C$, and the collapsed arc is an interior point of that disk. If the two end matchings agree, then $K/A$ is two closed disks joined at their interior centers, so it is not a topological two-manifold at the collapsed point. Explicitly, $K/A$ is the cone on the graph $C$; the latter is one four-edge circle for distinct matchings and two disjoint two-edge circles for equal matchings.

Consequently, if a finite Hausdorff two-dimensional cell complex is already a topological two-manifold away from finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes, with neighborhoods modeled by the interiors $r<1$ of these four-page models with distinct end matchings, collapsing those arcs gives a topological two-manifold. No boundary is created at a collapsed point. Collapsing any finite disjoint arc subcomplexes preserves the Euler characteristic, whether or not the local end matchings differ. These are intrinsic topological conclusions; an ambient embedding or local flatness needs separate data.

Let $\alpha:[-1,1]\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth embedding with nonvanishing derivative, smooth in boundary charts at both endpoints, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of its image $A$. Then there is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, whose only non-singleton fiber is $A$. In particular the quotient space $S^3/A$, obtained by identifying exactly the points of $A$ to one point, is homeomorphic to $S^3$.

Moreover there is a continuous family $Q:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3$ with $Q_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $Q_1=q$, fixed on $S^3\setminus U$, such that every $Q_t$ for $0\le t<1$ is a homeomorphism. Every closed parameter interval $[0,t_0]$ with $t_0<1$ therefore gives an ambient topological isotopy. The assertion concerns a topological quotient; it does not assert that the terminal map is a diffeomorphism or that an arbitrary surface containing the arc becomes a surface after collapse.

derivations.claim: Orient $\alpha$ from its first to its second endpoint, and extend this orientation to $A$. Along its open part choose continuous smooth transverse directions $u$ on $F_0$ and $v$ on $F_1$ so that the ordered triple $(\dot A,u,v)$ has positive ambient orientation. Such choices exist along an interval: choose the first direction in finite surface charts and interpolate consecutive signs consistently, and choose the sign of the second by the displayed orientation condition. Inside the radial collars these directions extend to nonzero boundary-tangent directions at the two points of $L$. To verify this, write the two collars as $(s,r,\theta_k(s))$. At a common radial arc their transverse tangents have base component $\partial_s$ and angular component $r\theta_k'(s)$ in the oriented unit angular direction of the normal disk. The boundary-curve transversality says $\theta_0'(s)-\theta_1'(s)\ne0$ there. Hence the orientation of their ordered transverse pair has constant nonzero sign for every $r>0$ and has a definite limiting sign choice on each copy of the boundary tangent at $r=0$. The individual directions remain transverse to $A$ on their own surfaces all the way to those endpoints.

These directions give relative strips on both surfaces. Extend the transverse field on each surface to a neighborhood of $A$, tangent to $L$ at its two ends, using finitely many surface charts and cutoffs. In the boundary charts take its restriction to $L$ to be a signed unit tangent for a common arclength parameter. Its short flow in [F1] sends $(t,r)$ to the time-$r$ point starting at $A(t)$; the two derivatives are independent on the zero section. By [F1], compactness and the same converging-collision argument as for a normal arc chart, it is an embedded rectangle for a sufficiently small uniform width. Uniqueness of the flow retains its two end edges on $L$. The positive and negative halves give two pages on each surface. By the isolated-intersection hypothesis, after shrinking they meet only along $A$ and their end edges on $L$. Their widths on these end edges can be chosen equal in the common arclength parameter, so the end identifications are pointwise in the page radius. Label the $u$-positive, $v$-positive, $u$-negative and $v$-negative pages by $0,1,2,3$. This gives exactly the asserted four-page neighborhood.

At either exterior endpoint project $u,v$ to its boundary torus along $\dot A$. These are nonzero tangent vectors parallel respectively to the two boundary curves: each surface tangent plane contains $\dot A$ and its boundary-curve tangent. Let $s_0,s_1\in\{1,-1\}$ record whether those projected directions agree with the chosen orientations of the respective boundary curves. Following the radial collars to $L$ retains precisely these signs relative to the common oriented boundary tangent, by the collar coordinates in step 1.1. The positive page on $F_0$ is therefore glued to the positive page on $F_1$ exactly when $s_0s_1=1$. If the product is negative it is glued to the negative page instead. Thus the matching at that endpoint is $M$ for product $1$ and $N$ for product $-1$. This assertion uses the signs separately at each endpoint, not a presumed orientation of either whole surface.

At the first endpoint $\dot A$ points from the solid tube into $X$; at the second it points back toward the solid tube. Projection along $\dot A$ consequently carries the oriented transverse plane determined by $(\dot A,u,v)$ to the oriented torus plane with sign $+1$ at the first endpoint and $-1$ at the second. Indeed the solid tube boundary orientation is defined by putting its outward normal first, and that normal has respectively positive and negative component along $\dot A$. Therefore the two local boundary intersection signs are $i_0=s_0^{\mathrm{first}}s_1^{\mathrm{first}}$ and $i_1=-s_0^{\mathrm{second}}s_1^{\mathrm{second}}$. By step 3.1 the end matchings differ exactly when the two products differ. These displayed formulas show this is equivalent to $i_0=i_1$. Equal matchings occur exactly when $i_0=-i_1$.

Apply [F2] to the actual neighborhood in step 2.1. By step 4.1 the standard sign sums $2$ and $-2$ give its disk quotient, while sum zero gives the two-disk wedge. To realize the former quotient inside the ambient sphere use [F3] on the smooth arc $A$, with any prescribed neighborhood as support. Its restriction to the compact $K$ has exactly the same identifications as $K/A$. The induced map of that quotient onto its image in $S^3$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism. Its image is therefore an embedded topological disk. The construction has proved its intrinsic topology and its ambient embedding, while making no local-flatness conclusion at the collapsed point.
